idiom_name: wrapper class holding the interface + hand-written forwarders (explicit interface implementation for a private surface)
implementation_notes: C# has no by-like keyword for object delegation: the wrapper declares that it implements the interface and then writes each forwarder, and an explicit interface implementation (`void IStore.Save(string id) => _inner.Save(id);`) keeps forwarded members off the class's public surface entirely. The framework's delegation primitive is the callable (`Func`/`Action`, events), not the contained object, so hand-written interface forwarding is the default and remains right for a narrow, type-checked wrapper; for wide interfaces or interception the runtime alternative is `System.Reflection.DispatchProxy`, which generates an interface implementation that routes every call to one `Invoke` method.
pitfalls: An explicit interface implementation is invisible on the class: `new CountingStore(x).Save(id)` does not compile and the member cannot be called without an interface reference - a surprise for tests and DI registrations.
Forwarding by hand means the compiler helps only when the interface changes; members that exist on the delegate's concrete type but not on the interface simply are not part of the wrapper's contract.
`Func`/`Action`-based delegation is a different mechanism than interface delegation: it forwards calls, not identity, so `Equals`/`GetHashCode` semantics and `is`-checks are lost.

variants.name: DispatchProxy runtime forwarding
variants.idiom_name: DispatchProxy.Create<T, TProxy>() + Invoke forwarding to a wrapped target
variants.implementation_notes: DispatchProxy is the .NET Standard replacement for the retired RealProxy: `Create<T, TProxy>()` returns an instance of interface T whose every call is routed to the proxy's `Invoke(MethodInfo, object[])`, which can forward with `method.Invoke(target, args)`. It removes the per-member boilerplate and can wrap an object that already exists, but it proxies interfaces only - fields and non-interface members are unreachable - and calls the target makes to itself are not intercepted. Choose it for wide interfaces and interception-heavy wrappers; Castle.Core's DynamicProxy is the common third-party upgrade path when virtual-method or class proxying is needed.
pitfalls: DispatchProxy generates an interface-only proxy: members outside T and all fields are unavailable, so access needs reflection or helper methods on the proxy.
Self-calls inside the target (one method calling another member of the same object) are not proxied, so interception only covers external interface calls.
Every call goes through reflection and `Invoke`: slower than a written forwarder, and business exceptions arrive wrapped in `TargetInvocationException`.
